newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Zeeland's farmers fight to keep dykes, save land.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Zeeland's farmers fight to keep dykes, save land.

text.p: Ten years after the world's largest sea defence barrier was completed, environmentalists have enraged farmers by calling for dykes to be breached and hard-won land returned to the sea.

The multi-billion dollar barrier was built to prevent a repetition of the 1953 disaster in which nearly 2,000 people and thousands of farm animals were drowned when the North Sea, whipped up by gales and spring tides, smashed dykes in the low lying coastal region.
"It's crazy when there are so many people and so much pressure on land in the Netherlands," said Bas Seytel, secretary of the Zeeland farmers' union.
Environmentalists say the sea barriers and dykes have threatened the survival of coastal plants and wildlife.
The storm surge barrier at Oosterschelde is part of a huge coastal defence programme to protect the flood-prone Delta region where the Scheldt, Rhine and Maas rivers flow into the North Sea.
Until the 1960s Zeeland was a series of islands before being linked by a series of dams and bridges.
Now Zeeland boasts some of the country's most fertile soil, mainly flat farmland used for cereals, punctuated with huge apple and pear orchards.
Proximity to the sea reduces the risk of frost damage to fruit while nearby ports facilitate exports to Britain and Scandinavia.
COMPLAINTS ABOUT EU FARM POLICY
Like their counterparts across the continent, Zeeland's farmers complain about European Union farm policy.
A 50 percent decline in cereals support prices over the past 10 years has prompted farmers to grow more potatoes, onions and sugar beet.
"The market is glutted with these products and prices have dropped," complained Seytel.

Farmers have also been switching to pigs but with a serious outbreak of swine fever in the southeast of the country and pollution problems caused by pig slurry, Zeeland is wary about any large scale development.
"We don't want too many pigs crowding the land," Seytel said.

Farmers differ from industrial workers because they are tied to the land and cannot easily switch jobs when business is bad, he said, adding that they try to maintain earnings by increasing production which only makes the situation worse.
The number of farms in Zeeland has fallen by 10 percent since 1985 and one in five farmers now earns part of his living teaching in agricultural colleges, bus driving or as a postman.
An increasing number of farmers have opened small campsites for tourists who flock to the region's attractive sandy beaches.
PROBLEMS IN COMMON WITH OTHER EU COUNTRIES
Although Zeeland's farmers account for barely one percent of EU production they say their problems are mirrored across the EU's 15 member states.
Cereals are the pivotal crop and its problems are quickly passed on to other farming sectors.
When EU farm ministers met informally last month in Zeeland's historic capital, Middelburg, local farmers seized the opportunity to demand action to safeguard the cereals market.
They want an increase in the amount of land farmers must set aside in order to claim EU subsidies, saying this would curb production and strengthen prices.
At the same time they want assurances that payments to compensate for cuts in cereals support prices agreed under 1992 farm reforms, would be continued without preconditions.
They say that extra conditions, such as less fertiliser and pesticide and caring for the countryside, would create uncompetitive "museum" agriculture.
Cereals imports must be minimised while exports should be promoted by aggressive use of subsidies.
"A further and literal execution of the free trade principle will be fatal to European agriculture," they said in a statement referring to the rules of the World Trade Organisation.

But their demands failed to impress the EU's Austrian Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler who says that cereals farmers are over-subsidised and is seeking to slash aid payments by more than one billion dollars.

The EU has continued to compensate cereals farmers for a 30 percent cut in support prices agreed in 1992 even though they have been able to sell their grain at much higher levels for most of the time.
